## Proof

**Step 1: Locate $a_n$ precisely.** We have $P(x)=x^{n}(x-2)+1$, so $P(1)=0$ and $P(2)=1>0$. Also
$$P'(x)=x^{n-1}\bigl((n+1)x-2n\bigr),$$
hence $P$ is strictly decreasing on $\bigl(1,\tfrac{2n}{n+1}\bigr)$ and strictly increasing on $\bigl(\tfrac{2n}{n+1},+\infty\bigr)$. Since $P(1)=0$ and $P$ decreases on $\bigl(1,\tfrac{2n}{n+1}\bigr)$, we have $P<0$ there. Since $P\bigl(\tfrac{2n}{n+1}\bigr)<0$ and $P(2)=1>0$ with $P$ increasing on $\bigl(\tfrac{2n}{n+1},2\bigr)$, there is a unique root
$$a_n\in\Bigl(\tfrac{2n}{n+1},\,2\Bigr)\subset(1,2].$$
(The root $x=1$ is excluded by the open endpoint.) In particular, setting $t_n:=2-a_n$,
$$0<t_n<2-\tfrac{2n}{n+1}=\tfrac{2}{n+1},\qquad\text{so}\quad n\,t_n<\tfrac{2n}{n+1}<2.\tag{1}$$

**Step 2: Reformulate the equation.** From $P(a_n)=0$,
$$a_n^{\,n}(2-a_n)=1\quad\Longrightarrow\quad (2-t_n)^n\,t_n=1.$$
Factoring out $2^n$:
$$2^n\Bigl(1-\tfrac{t_n}{2}\Bigr)^{\!n}t_n=1 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad 2^n t_n=\Bigl(1-\tfrac{t_n}{2}\Bigr)^{\!-n}.$$
Define $s_n:=2^n t_n$. Then the desired limit is
$$L=\lim_{n\to\infty}2^n(2-a_n)=\lim_{n\to\infty}s_n,\qquad s_n=\Bigl(1-\tfrac{t_n}{2}\Bigr)^{\!-n},\quad t_n=\frac{s_n}{2^n}.\tag{2}$$

**Step 3: $s_n$ is bounded.** Taking logarithms in (2),
$$\ln s_n=-n\ln\Bigl(1-\tfrac{t_n}{2}\Bigr).$$
Since $t_n/2<1/(n+1)\le 1/3<1/2$ for $n\ge 2$, we use $-\ln(1-u)\le u+u^2$ (valid for $u\in[0,\tfrac12]$):
$$\ln s_n\le n\Bigl(\tfrac{t_n}{2}+\tfrac{t_n^2}{4}\Bigr)=\tfrac{n\,t_n}{2}+\tfrac{n\,t_n^2}{4}.$$
By (1), $n\,t_n<2$, and $n\,t_n^2=(n\,t_n)\cdot t_n<2\,t_n\to 0$. Hence
$$\ln s_n\le 1+o(1),\qquad\text{so } s_n\le e\,(1+o(1)):\; s_n\text{ is bounded}.\tag{3}$$

**Step 4: $s_n\to 1$.** From (3) and $t_n=s_n/2^n$,
$$n\,t_n=\frac{n\,s_n}{2^n}\to 0\qquad(\text{bounded}\times n/2^n).\tag{4}$$
Now expand the logarithm exactly:
$$\ln s_n=-n\ln\Bigl(1-\tfrac{t_n}{2}\Bigr)=n\Bigl(\tfrac{t_n}{2}+\tfrac{t_n^2}{8}+\cdots\Bigr)=\tfrac{n\,t_n}{2}+O\bigl(n\,t_n^2\bigr).$$
By (4), $\tfrac{n\,t_n}{2}\to 0$, and $n\,t_n^2=(n\,t_n)\cdot t_n\to 0\cdot 0=0$. Therefore
$$\ln s_n\to 0,\qquad\text{hence } s_n\to e^0=1.$$

Since $L=\lim_{n\to\infty}s_n$,

$$\boxed{L=1}.$$

## Proof

**Step 1: Locate $a_n$ precisely.** We have $P(x)=x^{n}(x-2)+1$, so $P(1)=0$ and $P(2)=1>0$. Also
$$P'(x)=x^{n-1}\bigl((n+1)x-2n\bigr),$$
hence $P$ is strictly decreasing on $\bigl(1,\tfrac{2n}{n+1}\bigr)$ and strictly increasing on $\bigl(\tfrac{2n}{n+1},+\infty\bigr)$. Since $P(1)=0$ and $P$ decreases on $\bigl(1,\tfrac{2n}{n+1}\bigr)$, we have $P<0$ there. Since $P\bigl(\tfrac{2n}{n+1}\bigr)<0$ and $P(2)=1>0$ with $P$ increasing on $\bigl(\tfrac{2n}{n+1},2\bigr)$, there is a unique root
$$a_n\in\Bigl(\tfrac{2n}{n+1},\,2\Bigr)\subset(1,2].$$
(The root $x=1$ is excluded by the open endpoint.) In particular, setting $t_n:=2-a_n$,
$$0<t_n<2-\tfrac{2n}{n+1}=\tfrac{2}{n+1},\qquad\text{so}\quad n\,t_n<\tfrac{2n}{n+1}<2.\tag{1}$$

**Step 2: Reformulate the equation.** From $P(a_n)=0$,
$$a_n^{\,n}(2-a_n)=1\quad\Longrightarrow\quad (2-t_n)^n\,t_n=1.$$
Factoring out $2^n$:
$$2^n\Bigl(1-\tfrac{t_n}{2}\Bigr)^{\!n}t_n=1 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad 2^n t_n=\Bigl(1-\tfrac{t_n}{2}\Bigr)^{\!-n}.$$
Define $s_n:=2^n t_n$. Then the desired limit is
$$L=\lim_{n\to\infty}2^n(2-a_n)=\lim_{n\to\infty}s_n,\qquad s_n=\Bigl(1-\tfrac{t_n}{2}\Bigr)^{\!-n},\quad t_n=\frac{s_n}{2^n}.\tag{2}$$

**Step 3: $s_n$ is bounded.** Taking logarithms in (2),
$$\ln s_n=-n\ln\Bigl(1-\tfrac{t_n}{2}\Bigr).$$
Since $t_n/2<1/(n+1)\le 1/3<1/2$ for $n\ge 2$, we use $-\ln(1-u)\le u+u^2$ (valid for $u\in[0,\tfrac12]$):
$$\ln s_n\le n\Bigl(\tfrac{t_n}{2}+\tfrac{t_n^2}{4}\Bigr)=\tfrac{n\,t_n}{2}+\tfrac{n\,t_n^2}{4}.$$
By (1), $n\,t_n<2$, and $n\,t_n^2=(n\,t_n)\cdot t_n<2\,t_n\to 0$. Hence
$$\ln s_n\le 1+o(1),\qquad\text{so } s_n\le e\,(1+o(1)):\; s_n\text{ is bounded}.\tag{3}$$

**Step 4: $s_n\to 1$.** From (3) and $t_n=s_n/2^n$,
$$n\,t_n=\frac{n\,s_n}{2^n}\to 0\qquad(\text{bounded}\times n/2^n).\tag{4}$$
Now expand the logarithm exactly:
$$\ln s_n=-n\ln\Bigl(1-\tfrac{t_n}{2}\Bigr)=n\Bigl(\tfrac{t_n}{2}+\tfrac{t_n^2}{8}+\cdots\Bigr)=\tfrac{n\,t_n}{2}+O\bigl(n\,t_n^2\bigr).$$
By (4), $\tfrac{n\,t_n}{2}\to 0$, and $n\,t_n^2=(n\,t_n)\cdot t_n\to 0\cdot 0=0$. Therefore
$$\ln s_n\to 0,\qquad\text{hence } s_n\to e^0=1.$$

Since $L=\lim_{n\to\infty}s_n$,

$$\boxed{L=1}.$$
